How to Write a Clear Email Opt-in Form

By the Northwind editorial team

An opt-in form is often the first promise a business makes to a new subscriber. If the promise is vague, people sign up expecting one thing and receive another, and the unsubscribe rate climbs within weeks. A clear form sets expectations before the first email is ever sent.

Say what people will receive

Name the content and the frequency in plain words, for example "a weekly roundup of three recipes" rather than "updates and offers". Readers decide in a few seconds, so the description should fit on one line next to the field. If you plan to send promotions as well as editorial content, say so on the form instead of adding them later.

Avoid pre-ticked boxes. A subscriber who ticks the box themselves has made a choice, and that choice is easier to show later if anyone asks how consent was collected. Keep a record of the date, the form version and the wording the person saw.

Ask only for what you need

Every extra field lowers the number of people who finish the form. For most newsletters an email address is enough at the start. If you want a first name for personalisation, make it optional and explain why you ask. Collect other details later, once the subscriber trusts you and can see the benefit.

Confirm and follow through

Send a short confirmation message straight away. It should repeat what the person signed up for, show when the next issue will arrive, and include a working unsubscribe link. A double opt-in, where the subscriber clicks a link to confirm, removes typing mistakes and keeps the list clean, although it costs a small share of sign-ups.

Finally, test the form on a phone. Many people sign up from a mobile screen, where long legal text and tiny checkboxes are hard to use. A form that is easy to read on a small screen is usually easy to read everywhere else too.
